title.value: Fractures in Entrada Sandstone Arches National Park, Utah

note.value:
Nearly-unreformed rocks on the SW limb of the Salt Valley anticline in eastern Utah have been subjected to a remarkably varied loading history. The rocks contain many types of fractures: pristine joints and faults, joints that have become faults, and faults that have become joints. Thetraces define at least three sets of essentially vertical fractures (Fig. 1). Although all the faults are strike-slip faults (Dyer, 1983; Zhao and Johnson, 1990a,b), there are two distinct types. One is the band fault described in porous sandstones by Aydinand others (e.g., Dunn, LaFountain and Jackson, 1973; Aydin, 1978; Aydin and Johnson, 1978, 1983; Smith, 1983). The other is the faulted joint, described by Segall, Pollard and oth- ers, (e.g., Segall and Pollard, 1983b; Dyer, 1983; Davies and Pollard, 1986; Martel et al., 1988; Cruikshank, Zhao and Johnson, 1990a). Furthermore, both the faults and the joints are transformed structures so they behaved differently at different stages of the deformational history, much as demonstrated by Fleming and Johnson (1989) in landslides in Utah.

The Garden Area provides excellent exposures of fractures that were arrested in different stages of development. The fractures occur within about ten meters of white sandstone, the Moab Member of the Entrada Sandstone. Underlying the white sandstone are 70 to 95 m of red, cross-bedded sandstone of the Slick-rock Member of the Entrada Sandstone and overlying are about 12 m of thinly-interbedded clay stone, sand- stone, and limestone of the lower pan of the Morrison Formation (Dyer, 1983).

The purposes of this study were to describe the fractures, particularly their regional patterns, and to interpret the fracture patterns in terms of regional and local deformations accommodated by the formation and subsequent deformation of the fractures. The development of individual structures is addressed through detailed study of their forms and by mechanical analysis. We then deduce the regional evolution of the structures.
Cruikshank, Kenneth M. (1990). Fractures in Entrada Sandstone Arches National Park, Utah. Stanford Digital Repository. Available at: http://purl.stanford.edu/xz706vz4874
